Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Being reminded of the event by others

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I have to be on guard all the time
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The appraisal of permanent bodily damage is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context. The other selected items consistently reflect ongoing external danger and hyperarousal (world dangerous, on guard, startle, false alarms, threat in silence) plus intrusive sensory memory, but there are no corroborating memory, threat, or strategy items indicating injury-focused trauma consequences, pain, disability, or body-related threat. For a refugee trauma profile, this isolated somatic-damage belief is not impossible, but in this item set it stands out as clinically incoherent with the dominant formulation of danger-based threat and avoidance.

vignette:
Ethan Miller was eleven years old when his family fled their home in the middle of the night. The civil war had reached their town, and the gunfire that had been distant for months was suddenly in the street outside. He remembered the smell of diesel from the truck they were loaded into, the way his mother pressed his head down against her chest so he couldn't see, the long hours of silence while they hid in the back while the engine idled at a checkpoint. Nobody spoke. The silence itself had felt like a held breath, heavy with the possibility that a soldier would yank open the tarpaulin and everything would end. That silence stayed with him. Years later, resettled in the United States, Ethan's life looked nothing like that night. He had worked hard, put himself through law school, and at twenty-one he had become one of the youngest public defenders in the city. His girlfriend, Mia, was proud of him; his colleagues respected his fierce advocacy for clients who often had nowhere else to turn. But the old vigilance had never left. He had come to believe that the world was inherently dangerous, that safety was an illusion, and that he had to be on guard at all times because you never knew what could happen next. At work, he had learned to keep his voice low and his movements controlled. A door slamming in the courthouse corridor made him jolt so hard that coffee sometimes spilled on his files. The first time it happened, a senior attorney laughed and said, "Nervous, Miller?" Ethan forced a smile, but his heart was pounding and his palms were slick. He had learned to anticipate those sounds, scanning hallways before walking through them, checking exits in every room. He was certain that the smallest lapse in attention could cost him everything.

His caseload included asylum seekers, and that was the hardest part. When a new client described the border crossing-the silence of the desert, the sudden lights of a patrol vehicle-Ethan felt his body lock into the same crouched position he had held in that truck. His knees ached. He could see the image, vivid and wordless: the tarpaulin, the darkness, his father's hand gripping his arm so tightly it left bruises. Sometimes the full emotional wave would hit him without any picture at all-just a crushing terror that came from nowhere, leaving him disoriented for minutes afterward. He had grown terrified of his own mind. He found himself constantly monitoring his thoughts, checking for signs that he was losing control, that he might break down in front of a judge or a client. Avoidance had become second nature. He made excuses when colleagues asked about his background-"I don't really talk about it" became his standard reply. He unfollowed news accounts that covered war or displacement. When Mia once mentioned a documentary about refugees, he told her he had a headache and left the room. She had started to notice. They used to talk easily, but now he deflected, and she worried that he was pushing her away. He worried too, but the thought of explaining felt impossible; it would mean reopening the silence.

The worst moments came at night. He would lie awake, listening to the quiet of the apartment, and the silence itself felt threatening-a precursor to something terrible. He would snap at a creak in the floorboards, his heart racing, even though he knew rationally that nothing was wrong. Mia tried to comfort him, but he could not explain why his body refused to settle. He was afraid he was going crazy. Finally, after he had to excuse himself from a client meeting because a sudden, image-less panic attack had left him shaking, his supervisor pulled him aside and quietly suggested he see a therapist. Ethan agreed. He sat in the waiting room now, hands cold, knowing that the only thing worse than talking about the truck and the silence would be living with it forever. What frightened him most was the possibility that if he let his guard down, he would never get it back-and then he would be exactly as vulnerable as he had been at eleven. But something else, smaller and newer, was a hope that he might someday sit in silence and hear only the ordinary stillness of his own life.
